solutions.text: Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. My father had an authoritarian style and expected all of us to obey him without any argument. — AUTHORITARIAN (adj) = độc đoán, đòi hỏi tuân phục tuyệt đối; collocation chuẩn "an authoritarian style/parent/approach". Dễ nhầm với "authoritative" (có uy tín, được tin tưởng) — hai từ khác nghĩa hoàn toàn.

2. After the two brothers stopped speaking for years, a deep estrangement grew between them. — ESTRANGEMENT (n) = sự xa cách, rạn nứt tình cảm; đi với giới từ "estranged FROM" (không phải "with"). Danh từ trừu tượng, không đếm được.

3. My sister and I experienced intense sibling rivalry as we competed for our parents' attention. — SIBLING RIVALRY (n) = sự ganh đua giữa anh chị em; không đếm được ở nghĩa chung, tránh nói "a sibling rivalries".

4. The young couple went through a period of cohabitation for two years before they finally got married. — COHABITATION (n) = sống chung như vợ chồng khi chưa kết hôn; động từ tương ứng là "cohabit", không phải "cohabitate".

5. In many Asian households, filial piety dictates that children care for their parents out of duty and respect. — FILIAL PIETY (n) = lòng hiếu thảo; thường đi với "a deep sense of filial piety" hoặc "rooted in filial piety". "Filial" luôn là tính từ, không đứng độc lập như danh từ.
6. From a very young age, my grandmother inculcated in us the importance of honesty. — INCULCATE (v) = gieo rèn, thấm nhuần; cấu trúc chuẩn "inculcate sth IN/INTO sb", KHÔNG phải "inculcate sb sth".

7. Intergenerational conflicts over technology and values are increasingly common. — INTERGENERATIONAL (adj) = liên thế hệ; viết liền, không tách thành "inter-generation". Thường đi với "conflict/gap/household".
8. Some parents find it hard to grant their teenagers autonomy. — AUTONOMY (n) = quyền tự chủ; danh từ không đếm được, tính từ tương ứng là "autonomous" (không phải "autonomic").

9. Many people in their forties now belong to the sandwich generation, caring for both ageing parents and young children at once. — SANDWICH GENERATION (n) = thế hệ bị kẹp giữa; luôn dùng với mạo từ xác định "THE sandwich generation", không chia số nhiều.

10. Some experts believe that a lack of parental supervision can lead teenagers into delinquency. — DELINQUENCY (n) = hành vi phạm pháp/lệch chuẩn ở thanh thiếu niên; danh từ trừu tượng, người thực hiện gọi là "a delinquent". Thường thấy trong cụm "juvenile delinquency".

11. People often say that I bear a striking resemblance to my mother at my age. — BEAR A STRIKING RESEMBLANCE (phrase) = giống nhau rõ rệt; cấu trúc "bear a resemblance TO sb", tránh dùng lối khẩu ngữ "spitting image" trong văn phong trang trọng.

12. My younger brother followed in our father's footsteps and studied medicine. — FOLLOW IN SOMEONE'S FOOTSTEPS (idiom) = nối nghiệp, tiếp bước; luôn cần tính từ sở hữu trước "footsteps" ("in HIS footsteps"), không bỏ qua.
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Grandparents frequently take on childcare duties so that both parents can continue working full-time.
Band 8: In many dual-income households, it falls to grandparents to shoulder much of the childcare burden, quietly passing down family values in the process. (reduced relative + nominalisation)
2. Band 7: Children raised in a nurturing environment tend to grow into confident, well-adjusted adults.
Band 8: So formative is a nurturing upbringing that its imprint on a child's confidence can still be discerned decades into adulthood. (inversion of "so + adj")
3. Band 7: My mother seems to sense my mood instinctively, even when I say nothing at all.
Band 8: Such is my mother's maternal instinct that she invariably senses my mood long before a single word passes my lips. (inversion + hedging)
4. Band 7: Marriage rates have declined significantly compared with those of previous generations.
Band 8: Not only have marriage rates fallen sharply across recent generations, but cohabitation has also emerged as a widely accepted alternative. (negative inversion)
5. Band 7: It is essential for parents to devote quality time to their children on a daily basis.
Band 8: Were parents to prioritise quality time over material provision, the emotional bond within the family would, in all likelihood, be considerably stronger. (conditional inversion "Were... to")
6. Band 7: Even children who come from a broken home can go on to lead successful, fulfilled lives.
Band 8: It is not the intactness of the family unit but the quality of emotional support that ultimately determines whether a child from a broken home thrives. (cleft sentence)
7. Band 7: As life expectancy rises, more families are confronting the challenge of caring for elderly relatives.

Band 8: Deeply embedded in the notion of filial piety, the responsibility of caring for one's ageing forebears is becoming an ever more pressing concern as life expectancy climbs. (reduced relative + nominalisation)
8. Band 7: Siblings sometimes drift apart emotionally as they grow older and relocate.
Band 8: Were siblings to go years without meeting, the kinship they share would not necessarily be diminished, though the day-to-day intimacy inevitably would. (conditional inversion)

passages.text: The phrase "sandwich generation" was coined in 1981 by Dorothy Miller, a social worker at the University of Kentucky, to describe adults — predominantly women in their forties and fifties — squeezed between the obligation of supporting elderly parents and that of raising still-dependent children. For nearly two decades the term circulated mostly within professional journals. By the mid-2000s, demographic shifts in industrial economies had transformed what had been a niche category into a statistically significant cohort. Census data from the United States, Japan and Italy converged on a striking pattern: roughly one adult in seven aged forty to fifty-nine was providing routine assistance to a parent over sixty-five while also financially supporting at least one child under twenty-five. The figure has prompted what Professor Carol Levine of the United Hospital Fund describes as "a quiet reorganisation of mid-life expectations".

The conventional explanation rests on two converging trends. Life expectancy in high-income countries has risen by roughly twelve years since 1960, extending the period during which elderly parents may require some form of practical or financial assistance. Simultaneously, the postponement of childbearing into the early thirties — driven by extended schooling, female participation in the labour market and the rising cost of urban housing — has stretched the window during which adult children remain at home or partially dependent. The intersection of these two delays produces what demographers term a "vertical compression" of family obligations: caregiving demands that would historically have been spread across four or five adults are now concentrated, in many households, on one or two.

Yet a more sceptical analysis has emerged from researchers who consider the conventional account too tidy. Dr Aisha Ramaswamy, a sociologist at the London School of Economics, has argued that the sandwich-generation narrative obscures considerable variation across countries and class strata. In her 2019 study of 4,200 mid-life adults across nine European nations, Ramaswamy found that the genuine simultaneity of upward and downward caregiving — that is, intensive provision to both generations in the same week — was reported by only 8 per cent of respondents, well below the figure commonly quoted in policy debates. The remaining cases involved either rotational rather than simultaneous obligations or financial transfers without hands-on care. Conflating these distinct experiences, she contends, has inflated the perceived prevalence of the syndrome and may have distorted policy responses.

A second strand of revisionist work centres on the gendered architecture of the burden. Studies conducted at the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology indicate that, even where male and female respondents report comparable hours of care, the cognitive labour — scheduling medical appointments, anticipating future needs, managing intergenerational communication — falls disproportionately on women. Professor Mireille Drouet, who led the German arm of the project, observes that this invisible coordination resists conventional measurement and that surveys relying on diary entries systematically underestimate it. The implication, in her view, is that headline statistics on caregiving hours may understate the strain reported by women by something in the order of 30 per cent.

The economic consequences have only recently been quantified with any precision. Working-age caregivers who reduce their professional hours to manage dual obligations forgo, on average, future earnings equivalent to roughly 4 to 6 per cent of lifetime income, according to a 2021 analysis by the OECD. Pension contributions decline correspondingly, with knock-on effects for the caregiver's own old age. Crucially, the loss is not evenly distributed: middle-income women in their late forties absorb a markedly larger share than higher-earning men in the same age band, partly because their employment patterns are more flexible and partly because cultural expectations channel routine caregiving towards them.

These findings have prompted divergent policy responses. Sweden and the Netherlands have expanded paid leave entitlements that may be drawn down across multiple care recipients, in effect treating the sandwich condition as a recognised social risk. Japan, confronting a much steeper demographic curve, has invested heavily in robotic and digital assistance designed to substitute for some routine caregiving tasks, although uptake has remained modest. The United Kingdom and the United States, by contrast, have generally relied on tax credits and informal community provision, an approach that Professor Levine characterises as "structurally under-engineered". Whether any of these models will prove portable to economies with weaker welfare infrastructure remains an open question.

Several researchers caution against framing the sandwich generation primarily as a problem to be solved. Dr Hiro Yamamura, a gerontologist at Kyoto University, points to longitudinal evidence suggesting that adults who navigate the dual role report a slightly elevated sense of purpose and stronger intergenerational bonds, provided that external support is sufficient to prevent burnout. Where support is inadequate, the same caregivers display measurably higher rates of depressive symptoms. The most defensible position, Yamamura suggests, is that the sandwich condition is neither inherently harmful nor benign, but sharply sensitive to the surrounding institutional scaffolding.

What emerges is a more nuanced picture than the 1981 formulation allowed. The sandwich generation is real, but it is smaller, more gendered, more class-stratified and more dependent on national policy than early commentary suggested. Forecasting the next phase requires attention not only to demographic curves but to how societies share the work of caring across families, workplaces and the state.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we're, um, hearing from Priya and Oliver on intergenerational research methodology. Priya, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname for me?
Yeah, sure. So I'm Priya Sandhu — that's S-A-N-D-H-U, the H is silent. My project was a longitudinal study tracking forty-eight grandparent-grandchild dyads across the Lakeshore region. (Q1)

Erm, the pilot ran in 2019 — sorry, no, 2018 — and the main wave concluded in 2022. So four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2021, but the pandemic, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Tense-wise, just to clarify for the recording — your data collection FINISHED in 2022, and you're publishing this year, correct?
Right. Published 2026, but the next wave we're gonna run starts in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens here is what Susan Bengtson called the "intergenerational solidarity framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: kinship cohesion, family closeness, generational continuity. All those describe the same construct. The current scholarly term, though, is intergenerational solidarity. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Priya's framing. In my sample — twenty-nine households across Brisbane suburbs — most of the grandparents said they engage in childcare AT LEAST three times a week. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — twenty-two out of twenty-nine, so roughly seventy-six per cent. Only a few — about ten per cent — never did regular childcare, and some — fourteen per cent — did it sporadically. (Q4)
Right. Now, Priya, did your sample confirm the "grandparents-as-default-carers" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the dyads I observed did NOT regard grandparental childcare as obligatory. The implicit cultural contract, well, has shifted. Today's grandparents see it as a choice, not a duty. Only a small minority — fewer than fifteen per cent — described any sense of obligation. (Q5)

And, dunno about you, but I found something interesting on the helicopter-parenting axis. So-called intensive grandparenting — where grandparents replicate the hovering style — that's actually rising sharply in higher-income suburbs. And the literature suggests this constrains a child's capacity for autonomous problem-solving.
Hmm. Priya, did you control for socio-economic stratum?
Kinda. We stratified by income quartile. Counter-intuitively, the BOTTOM quartile reported the highest levels of grandparental involvement, not the top.
Well, it's about resource substitution — cheaper than paid childcare, so families lean on grandparents harder.

And one final thing — sibling rivalry data. In smaller families with two children, rivalry intensity was, um, considerably higher than in households of four-plus children. Researchers attribute it to scarcity of parental bandwidth.

Right. Now, going back to what Priya mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Oliver, on your seventy-six-per-cent figure: the implication that grandparents are de facto childminders aligns with Bengtson, but Priya's obligation finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: The line graph illustrates how the proportions of four household types changed in a European country between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the period was marked by two contrasting movements: the traditional married household and the multi-generational household both declined, whereas cohabiting couples and single-parent units rose substantially. By the close of the period, the rank order of the categories had been considerably reshuffled.

In 1980, married couples commanded the lion's share of households at 70%, with multi-generational families accounting for 15%. The married figure then fell continuously, dropping to 62% by 1990, 52% in 2000 and just 38% by 2020. The intergenerational household dwindled more gently, slipping from 15% to a marginal 9% over the four decades and ending as the smallest of the four categories.

By contrast, cohabiting couples surged sixfold, climbing from 5% to 30%, while single-parent units more than doubled, rising from 10% to 23%. Cohabiting and single-parent households both stood at 18% in 2000, but cohabitation then pulled away strongly. By 2020, it had risen to 30% and had come to challenge the married unit's long-standing dominance.
The line graph delineates shifts in the share of four household categories in a European country across the four decades from 1980 to 2020.

Overall, the data trace a quiet reconfiguration of the household landscape: the once-dominant married unit and the multi-generational household receded steadily, whereas cohabiting and single-parent arrangements proliferated. By the close of the period, the traditional hierarchy of family forms had been all but inverted.

Married couples, which had commanded fully 70% of households in 1980, contracted relentlessly to 62% by 1990, 52% by 2000 and to a mere 38% by 2020 — a loss of nearly half their original share. Multi-generational living dwindled more modestly, easing from 15% to a marginal 9%, thereby ending as the slenderest category of the four.

The risers described the inverse trajectory. Cohabitation surged sixfold, from a negligible 5% to a substantial 30%, while single-parent units more than doubled, from 10% to 23%. The two converged at 18% in 2000 before cohabitation accelerated away, climbing to 30% and drawing level with the married unit's eroding pre-eminence by the close of the period.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The question of whether children succeed mainly because of how they are raised or because of the genes they inherit has long divided researchers. While both clearly matter, I am inclined to believe that upbringing plays the more decisive role.

On the one hand, those who emphasise genetics point to twin studies. Identical twins separated at birth, for instance, often display strikingly similar levels of intelligence and temperament even when their environments differ greatly. This finding suggests a strong biological baseline, and it arguably explains why siblings raised in the same household, exposed to the same rules and resources, can nonetheless turn out so differently. From this perspective, parents may refine a child's behaviour, but the underlying genetic predisposition tends to dominate long-term outcomes such as temperament and aptitude.

On the other hand, supporters of nurture stress the influence of authoritative parenting, schooling and socio-economic context. Children growing up in dysfunctional homes frequently struggle academically regardless of their innate ability. The well-documented thirty-million-word gap between professional and low-income families illustrates how early input shapes vocabulary and thinking during the formative years. Crucially, the cognitive recovery of adopted orphans, who often catch up dramatically once placed with attentive families, shows that a supportive environment can compensate for a difficult start.

In my view, although genes set the outer ceiling of a child's potential, it is the upbringing that determines how close he or she comes to reaching it. A gifted child in a neglectful home rarely flourishes, whereas a child of average ability raised by attentive parents may succeed beyond expectation. For this reason, governments should arguably invest heavily in the early-years environment, since it offers the most efficient lever for improving children's outcomes.

Whether a child's eventual achievements stem primarily from upbringing or from inherited endowment has long been contested in developmental psychology. Notwithstanding the appeal of either extreme, I shall argue that nature and nurture operate interdependently, with the rearing environment functioning as the primary mediator that activates, suppresses or refines underlying genetic dispositions.

Advocates of the hereditarian position draw, not without justification, on robust behavioural-genetics evidence. The finding that identical twins reared apart show correlations exceeding 0.70 for cognitive ability intuitively favours a biological baseline, and it is this body of research that has resurrected polygenic scoring as a putative predictor of educational attainment. Compelling as such data appear, however, the inference that genes alone dictate destiny rests on assumptions about uniform environments that rarely hold in practice, for no two upbringings are ever truly identical.

Proponents of nurture, by the same token, marshal equally formidable evidence. Were genes wholly deterministic, the cognitive recovery of adopted orphans, documented across longitudinal cohorts, would simply not be observable. Moreover, parents who consciously inculcate self-regulation and intellectual curiosity appear to widen the very window through which genetic potential can express itself — a phenomenon increasingly framed as gene-environment correlation. The thirty-million-word gap between affluent and disadvantaged households illustrates how decisively early linguistic input can entrench or erode a child's later prospects.

In my considered view, the dichotomy is itself misleading. Genes may load the proverbial gun, but it is attentive upbringing, contingent upon socio-emotional scaffolding, that pulls the trigger. Particularly during the first five years, when synaptic pruning is most rapid, the rearing environment exerts a disproportionate influence. Policy should accordingly privilege early-years investment over deterministic narratives, recognising that the genome alone scripts no child's biography.

A. SENTENCE UPGRADE LADDER (Band 6 → 7 → 8)
Example 1 — Resemblance

solutions.text: Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. My father had an authoritarian style and expected all of us to obey him without any argument. — AUTHORITARIAN (adj) = độc đoán, đòi hỏi tuân phục tuyệt đối; collocation chuẩn "an authoritarian style/parent/approach". Dễ nhầm với "authoritative" (có uy tín, được tin tưởng) — hai từ khác nghĩa hoàn toàn.

2. After the two brothers stopped speaking for years, a deep estrangement grew between them. — ESTRANGEMENT (n) = sự xa cách, rạn nứt tình cảm; đi với giới từ "estranged FROM" (không phải "with"). Danh từ trừu tượng, không đếm được.

3. My sister and I experienced intense sibling rivalry as we competed for our parents' attention. — SIBLING RIVALRY (n) = sự ganh đua giữa anh chị em; không đếm được ở nghĩa chung, tránh nói "a sibling rivalries".

4. The young couple went through a period of cohabitation for two years before they finally got married. — COHABITATION (n) = sống chung như vợ chồng khi chưa kết hôn; động từ tương ứng là "cohabit", không phải "cohabitate".

5. In many Asian households, filial piety dictates that children care for their parents out of duty and respect. — FILIAL PIETY (n) = lòng hiếu thảo; thường đi với "a deep sense of filial piety" hoặc "rooted in filial piety". "Filial" luôn là tính từ, không đứng độc lập như danh từ.
6. From a very young age, my grandmother inculcated in us the importance of honesty. — INCULCATE (v) = gieo rèn, thấm nhuần; cấu trúc chuẩn "inculcate sth IN/INTO sb", KHÔNG phải "inculcate sb sth".

7. Intergenerational conflicts over technology and values are increasingly common. — INTERGENERATIONAL (adj) = liên thế hệ; viết liền, không tách thành "inter-generation". Thường đi với "conflict/gap/household".
8. Some parents find it hard to grant their teenagers autonomy. — AUTONOMY (n) = quyền tự chủ; danh từ không đếm được, tính từ tương ứng là "autonomous" (không phải "autonomic").

9. Many people in their forties now belong to the sandwich generation, caring for both ageing parents and young children at once. — SANDWICH GENERATION (n) = thế hệ bị kẹp giữa; luôn dùng với mạo từ xác định "THE sandwich generation", không chia số nhiều.

10. Some experts believe that a lack of parental supervision can lead teenagers into delinquency. — DELINQUENCY (n) = hành vi phạm pháp/lệch chuẩn ở thanh thiếu niên; danh từ trừu tượng, người thực hiện gọi là "a delinquent". Thường thấy trong cụm "juvenile delinquency".

11. People often say that I bear a striking resemblance to my mother at my age. — BEAR A STRIKING RESEMBLANCE (phrase) = giống nhau rõ rệt; cấu trúc "bear a resemblance TO sb", tránh dùng lối khẩu ngữ "spitting image" trong văn phong trang trọng.

12. My younger brother followed in our father's footsteps and studied medicine. — FOLLOW IN SOMEONE'S FOOTSTEPS (idiom) = nối nghiệp, tiếp bước; luôn cần tính từ sở hữu trước "footsteps" ("in HIS footsteps"), không bỏ qua.
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Grandparents frequently take on childcare duties so that both parents can continue working full-time.
Band 8: In many dual-income households, it falls to grandparents to shoulder much of the childcare burden, quietly passing down family values in the process. (reduced relative + nominalisation)
2. Band 7: Children raised in a nurturing environment tend to grow into confident, well-adjusted adults.
Band 8: So formative is a nurturing upbringing that its imprint on a child's confidence can still be discerned decades into adulthood. (inversion of "so + adj")
3. Band 7: My mother seems to sense my mood instinctively, even when I say nothing at all.
Band 8: Such is my mother's maternal instinct that she invariably senses my mood long before a single word passes my lips. (inversion + hedging)
4. Band 7: Marriage rates have declined significantly compared with those of previous generations.
Band 8: Not only have marriage rates fallen sharply across recent generations, but cohabitation has also emerged as a widely accepted alternative. (negative inversion)
5. Band 7: It is essential for parents to devote quality time to their children on a daily basis.
Band 8: Were parents to prioritise quality time over material provision, the emotional bond within the family would, in all likelihood, be considerably stronger. (conditional inversion "Were... to")
6. Band 7: Even children who come from a broken home can go on to lead successful, fulfilled lives.
Band 8: It is not the intactness of the family unit but the quality of emotional support that ultimately determines whether a child from a broken home thrives. (cleft sentence)
7. Band 7: As life expectancy rises, more families are confronting the challenge of caring for elderly relatives.

Band 8: Deeply embedded in the notion of filial piety, the responsibility of caring for one's ageing forebears is becoming an ever more pressing concern as life expectancy climbs. (reduced relative + nominalisation)
8. Band 7: Siblings sometimes drift apart emotionally as they grow older and relocate.
Band 8: Were siblings to go years without meeting, the kinship they share would not necessarily be diminished, though the day-to-day intimacy inevitably would. (conditional inversion)

The relative I'd genuinely love to forge a deeper connection with is my paternal uncle, Khanh — a rather enigmatic figure on my father's side of the family. What strikes me most about him is the quiet intensity he carries, almost as though every conversation conceals a hidden chapter. (cleft)

We only cross paths a couple of times a year, typically during Tet and the occasional summer visit to Da Lat, where he runs a modest coffee plantation. Were I to live closer, I'm convinced our relationship would have flourished by now; geography, however, has kept us at arm's length. (conditional inversion)

From what I've gleaned through family anecdotes, Uncle Khanh is something of an autodidact — he never attended university, yet he taught himself fluent French and has an encyclopaedic grasp of botany. Raised during the lean post-war years, he developed a stoicism that, as far as I can tell, has shaped his entire worldview. (reduced relative + hedging)

The reason I'd like to know him better is essentially twofold. First, he embodies a kind of kinship with our ancestral roots that's increasingly rare in my generation — the cultivation of filial piety, the preservation of dialect, the small rituals around tea. Second, not only does he possess a wealth of untold family history, but he also exemplifies the resilience I aspire to cultivate. (negative inversion + nominalisation)

Frankly, he's the black sheep turned quiet sage — to borrow an idiom (informal register). It strikes me that spending a fortnight in Da Lat with him would, in all likelihood, be more enlightening than any self-help book I've ever read. (hedging)

blocks.text: Q1. How important is family structure for child development?
P (Point): The structure of the family unit is, in my view, a foundational determinant of a child's psychological and cognitive trajectory, though far from the sole one.

E (Explanation): A stable structure provides the predictability and emotional scaffolding required for healthy attachment formation, which in turn shapes everything from self-regulation to academic engagement.

E (Example): A landmark OECD report (2022) on family transitions found that children raised in stable two-parent households outperformed peers from highly disrupted family configurations by roughly 0.4 standard deviations on PISA literacy scores. Likewise, the Harvard Grant Study, a 75-year longitudinal investigation, concluded that warm familial relationships in childhood were the single strongest predictor of adult wellbeing — eclipsing even socioeconomic status.
L (Link): Hence, while structure alone doesn't guarantee outcomes, its absence undeniably tilts the developmental odds.
Hedging Toolbox: one could reasonably argue / there is mounting evidence to suggest / by and large
Lexical Upgrade Box:
important → pivotal / formative
grow up → be raised in the formative years
family structure → familial configuration / household composition
Sample Answer (95 words):

There's mounting evidence to suggest that family structure exerts a formative influence on child development, particularly during the early years when the brain is most malleable. The Harvard Grant Study (2017 update) demonstrated that warm parent-child relationships were a more powerful predictor of adult flourishing than IQ or class. That said, one could reasonably argue it's the quality of attachment rather than structure per se that matters; a single-parent household imbued with love arguably outperforms a nuclear family riddled with conflict. By and large, both structure and emotional climate are inextricably linked.
Q2. Should adult children take care of elderly parents?
P: Adult children shoulder a moral, if not legal, obligation to care for their ageing parents, although the modality of that care must adapt to twenty-first-century realities.
E: This duty, rooted in reciprocity and filial piety, becomes ever more pressing as life expectancy rises and pension systems strain under demographic pressure.

E: According to the WHO World Report on Ageing (2015, updated 2020), the global population aged 60+ will hit 2.1 billion by 2050, with informal family care still constituting the dominant model of eldercare across Asia. In Vietnam, General Statistics Office data (2023) indicates roughly 70% of the elderly co-reside with adult children. Yet OECD's 2021 "Health at a Glance" warns that uncompensated family caregivers, predominantly women, face elevated burnout and depression rates.
L: Therefore, the responsibility ought to be a shared one — between adult offspring and a well-resourced state safety net.
Hedging Toolbox: it stands to reason that / arguably / to a considerable extent
Lexical Upgrade Box:
take care of → shoulder the caregiving burden
old people → the elderly / ageing population
children → adult offspring / the younger generation
Sample Answer (97 words):

It stands to reason that adult offspring shoulder a moral duty to support their ageing parents, especially in cultures steeped in filial piety like Vietnam. WHO's 2020 ageing report projects 2.1 billion people over 60 by 2050, and family caregiving will remain indispensable. However, this can't fall solely on individuals; the OECD (2021) flagged that informal caregivers — disproportionately women — suffer chronic burnout. Arguably, a hybrid model is optimal: emotional and financial responsibility from children, paired with state-subsidised home care. Not only does this preserve dignity, but it also prevents the caregiving generation from collapsing under the weight.
Q3. Will the nuclear family survive in 50 years?
P: The nuclear family, though far from obsolete, is being radically reconfigured and will likely persist only as one model among many by mid-century.
E: Plummeting fertility, the normalisation of cohabitation, single parenthood by choice, and chosen-family arrangements are eroding the hegemony of the mum-dad-two-kids template.

E: UN World Population Prospects (2022) projects that global fertility will fall below replacement (2.1) in most regions by 2070; South Korea already records 0.72 (Statistics Korea, 2024). The Pew Research Centre (2023) found that nearly 40% of US adults under 50 say they probably won't have children. Meanwhile, Eurostat (2023) reports that single-person households now constitute roughly 36% of all EU households — a historic high.
L: Hence, while the nuclear family won't disappear, it will surrender its status as the default to a far more pluralistic landscape.
Hedging Toolbox: in all likelihood / it would be premature to claim / on balance
Lexical Upgrade Box:
change → undergo a radical reconfiguration
fewer babies → plummeting fertility / sub-replacement fertility
normal family → the conventional nuclear template
Sample Answer (96 words):

In all likelihood, the nuclear family will endure but lose its monopoly. UN data (2022) shows fertility falling below 2.1 in most developed economies, and Pew (2023) found nearly 40% of younger Americans don't plan to have children. Eurostat (2023) likewise reports single-person households at 36% of the EU total. Were these trends to continue, what we now call "the family" will encompass cohabiting partners, single parents by choice, and chosen-family networks. It would be premature to claim the nuclear family is dying — but on balance, it's being dethroned as the default template.
T01 — FAMILY & UPBRINGING (Advanced C1, Band 7.5–8.0)
1. Section Type + Lecturer Info
Section: IELTS Listening Section 4 — extended academic monologue (no interruptions; one speaker for ~5 minutes)
Lecturer: Dr. Eleanor Whitfield, sociologist of family and ageing
Academic field: Sociology / Demography
Topic of lecture: "The Sandwich Generation: Dual-Income Households, Filial Piety and the Re-negotiation of Kinship Obligations"
2. Pre-listening Vocab Brush-up (Band 7+)
inculcate (v) — to instil an attitude or value through persistent teaching
progeny (n) — one's offspring, children collectively (formal)
kinship (n) — blood relationship; sense of family connection
delinquency (n) — minor criminal or anti-social behaviour, usually by the young
filial piety (n phrase) — duty / respect owed by children to parents
3. Predict 3 Ideas (Advanced)
The lecturer will probably define the "sandwich generation" as middle-aged adults caring simultaneously for ageing parents and dependent children.
She is likely to argue that dual-income households have eroded the traditional inculcation of filial piety.
A counter-argument may surface: extended kinship networks still serve as a buffer against juvenile delinquency in many cultures.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

Right, good morning everyone. Today's lecture continues our module on contemporary family structures, and I want to zoom in on a demographic cohort that sociologists rather evocatively call the "sandwich generation" — that is, adults, typically in their forties and fifties, who are squeezed, um, between caring for their elderly parents and raising their own progeny. [pause]

Now, historically, the inculcation of filial piety — particularly in East Asian contexts — meant that the burden of elder care was, well, an unquestioned moral obligation. However, with the rise of dual-income households since the 1980s, the dynamics of kinship have been profoundly re-negotiated. Both spouses pursue careers, and consequently, the so-called formative years of children are increasingly outsourced to childcare institutions or, indeed, to grandparents. [pause]

What's striking — and this is the crux of today's session — is that researchers initially predicted a sharp rise in juvenile delinquency as a direct corollary of parental absence. The data, however, tells a more nuanced story. Studies by the Pew Centre suggest that it isn't sheer time deprivation that correlates with antisocial behaviour; rather, it's the quality of attachment and the consistency of moral instruction. [pause]

Moreover, the boomerang phenomenon — adult children returning home due to exorbitant housing costs — has further complicated matters. Sandwich-generation parents now grapple with simultaneously fostering the autonomy of grown progeny and managing the cognitive decline of their own elders. The emotional toll, frankly, can be considerable. [pause]

Now, let me push this a little further, because there's a gendered dimension that the headline figures rather conveniently obscure. A longitudinal survey conducted by the MetLife Mature Market Institute tracked roughly twelve hundred caregivers over a decade, and what they found was, well, quite telling: women shoulder the lion's share of this dual burden. On average, daughters provided some forty per cent more hands-on care for ageing parents than sons did, and — this is the kicker — they were three times more likely to reduce their working hours or exit the labour force altogether. The cumulative lifetime cost in forgone wages and pensions, the researchers calculated, exceeded three hundred thousand dollars per woman. [pause]

A further consideration is what economists rather coldly term the "opportunity cost of love". If you like, the sandwich generation isn't simply tired — it's quietly haemorrhaging financial security. And here I'd urge you to resist the romantic assumption that co-residence with grandparents is always a panacea. Take the Chinese context, where the so-called 4-2-1 structure — four grandparents, two parents, one child — concentrates expectation onto a single offspring. Yes, grandparents often provide childcare, but in turn they demand reciprocal care later, and the intergenerational contract becomes, frankly, a fraught negotiation rather than a warm tradition. [pause]

What complicates this picture still further is geography. The atomisation of the modern family means adult children increasingly migrate for work, leaving what gerontologists call "distance-caregiving" households. One can hardly supervise a parent's medication over a video call. The emotional labour of guilt, of monitoring from afar, imposes its own psychological toll that the spreadsheets simply don't capture. [pause]

So, taking the demographic squeeze, the gendered inequity and the dispersal of kinship together, the implications for the welfare state are, I think, rather pressing. And that, of course, brings me to where we must turn next — let me flag the key policy implication…
Before we move on, let me flag the key policy implication: governments must invest in subsidised eldercare, otherwise the strain on this generation will, um, become demographically untenable.

7. Answer Key + "Listen for"

rows: Right after the phrase "demographic" — first technical term in the opening; falling intonation marks the keyword
Signpost "an unquestioned moral …" — slight emphasis on the noun that follows
Discourse marker "indeed" precedes a synonym chain; listen for the word stressed after "are increasingly"
Contrast cue "rather, it's the …" — the noun directly after "the" is the target

blocks.text: 8. Listening Skills Box

Signposting recognition: Phrases like "let me flag the key policy implication" (Q5) and "the crux of today's session" (Q4 context) explicitly mark high-yield answer zones. Train your ear to anticipate the noun phrase that follows.
Lexical reformulation: Q3 ("outsourced" = "delegated/handed over") requires recognising synonyms; in Section 4 the question word will almost never appear verbatim.
Hedge recognition: Words like "rather," "however," "actually" signal contrastive answers (Q4) — Cambridge Section 4 questions love this trap.
Numerical anchoring: "Since the 1980s" / "in their forties and fifties" function as orientation cues, not answers — don't be distracted.
Skills-to-question map: Skill 1 → Q5; Skill 2 → Q3; Skill 3 → Q4.

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~181 từ)
The line graph illustrates how the proportions of four household types changed in a European country between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the period was marked by two contrasting movements: the traditional married household and the multi-generational household both declined, whereas cohabiting couples and single-parent units rose substantially. By the close of the period, the rank order of the categories had been considerably reshuffled.

In 1980, married couples commanded the lion's share of households at 70%, with multi-generational families accounting for 15%. The married figure then fell continuously, dropping to 62% by 1990, 52% in 2000 and just 38% by 2020. The intergenerational household dwindled more gently, slipping from 15% to a marginal 9% over the four decades and ending as the smallest of the four categories.

By contrast, cohabiting couples surged sixfold, climbing from 5% to 30%, while single-parent units more than doubled, rising from 10% to 23%. Cohabiting and single-parent households both stood at 18% in 2000, but cohabitation then pulled away strongly. By 2020, it had risen to 30% and had come to challenge the married unit's long-standing dominance.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~181 từ)
The line graph delineates shifts in the share of four household categories in a European country across the four decades from 1980 to 2020.

Overall, the data trace a quiet reconfiguration of the household landscape: the once-dominant married unit and the multi-generational household receded steadily, whereas cohabiting and single-parent arrangements proliferated. By the close of the period, the traditional hierarchy of family forms had been all but inverted.

Married couples, which had commanded fully 70% of households in 1980, contracted relentlessly to 62% by 1990, 52% by 2000 and to a mere 38% by 2020 — a loss of nearly half their original share. Multi-generational living dwindled more modestly, easing from 15% to a marginal 9%, thereby ending as the slenderest category of the four.

The risers described the inverse trajectory. Cohabitation surged sixfold, from a negligible 5% to a substantial 30%, while single-parent units more than doubled, from 10% to 23%. The two converged at 18% in 2000 before cohabitation accelerated away, climbing to 30% and drawing level with the married unit's eroding pre-eminence by the close of the period.

T01 — FAMILY & UPBRINGING · Writing Task 2
(1) Đề bài

Đề bài.  Some people believe that a child's success depends mostly on the way they are brought up (nurture). Others believe that it is mainly determined by their genes (nature). Discuss both views and give your opinion.
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Phía nuôi dạy (nurture quyết định):
•  Phong cách nuôi dạy và kỷ luật trong những năm đầu đời định hình giá trị đạo đức (vd: trẻ được chăm sóc tiền-tiểu-học giàu kích thích có tỉ lệ tốt nghiệp cao hơn).
•  Bối cảnh kinh tế-xã hội định hình vốn từ và nhận thức — 'khoảng cách 30 triệu từ' giữa gia đình chuyên môn và gia đình thu nhập thấp.
•  Sang chấn hoặc điều kiện hóa giai đoạn đầu có thể lấn át khuynh hướng di truyền (vd: trẻ mồ côi được nhận nuôi phục hồi nhận thức rõ rệt).
Phía di truyền (gen quyết định):
•  Nghiên cứu song sinh tách nuôi cho thấy tương quan cao về IQ và tính cách dù môi trường khác nhau.
•  Khuynh hướng di truyền ảnh hưởng khí chất, nguy cơ rối loạn (ADHD, trầm cảm) và điểm đa-gen học vấn.
•  Trong cùng một gia đình, anh chị em được nuôi giống nhau vẫn cho kết quả rất khác — gợi ý yếu tố di truyền.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion

•  Body 1 — quan điểm di truyền: bằng chứng song sinh, khí chất, khác biệt anh chị em cùng nhà.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~283 words)

The question of whether children succeed mainly because of how they are raised or because of the genes they inherit has long divided researchers. While both clearly matter, I am inclined to believe that upbringing plays the more decisive role.

On the one hand, those who emphasise genetics point to twin studies. Identical twins separated at birth, for instance, often display strikingly similar levels of intelligence and temperament even when their environments differ greatly. This finding suggests a strong biological baseline, and it arguably explains why siblings raised in the same household, exposed to the same rules and resources, can nonetheless turn out so differently. From this perspective, parents may refine a child's behaviour, but the underlying genetic predisposition tends to dominate long-term outcomes such as temperament and aptitude.

On the other hand, supporters of nurture stress the influence of authoritative parenting, schooling and socio-economic context. Children growing up in dysfunctional homes frequently struggle academically regardless of their innate ability. The well-documented thirty-million-word gap between professional and low-income families illustrates how early input shapes vocabulary and thinking during the formative years. Crucially, the cognitive recovery of adopted orphans, who often catch up dramatically once placed with attentive families, shows that a supportive environment can compensate for a difficult start.

In my view, although genes set the outer ceiling of a child's potential, it is the upbringing that determines how close he or she comes to reaching it. A gifted child in a neglectful home rarely flourishes, whereas a child of average ability raised by attentive parents may succeed beyond expectation. For this reason, governments should arguably invest heavily in the early-years environment, since it offers the most efficient lever for improving children's outcomes.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~282 words)

Whether a child's eventual achievements stem primarily from upbringing or from inherited endowment has long been contested in developmental psychology. Notwithstanding the appeal of either extreme, I shall argue that nature and nurture operate interdependently, with the rearing environment functioning as the primary mediator that activates, suppresses or refines underlying genetic dispositions.

Advocates of the hereditarian position draw, not without justification, on robust behavioural-genetics evidence. The finding that identical twins reared apart show correlations exceeding 0.70 for cognitive ability intuitively favours a biological baseline, and it is this body of research that has resurrected polygenic scoring as a putative predictor of educational attainment. Compelling as such data appear, however, the inference that genes alone dictate destiny rests on assumptions about uniform environments that rarely hold in practice, for no two upbringings are ever truly identical.

Proponents of nurture, by the same token, marshal equally formidable evidence. Were genes wholly deterministic, the cognitive recovery of adopted orphans, documented across longitudinal cohorts, would simply not be observable. Moreover, parents who consciously inculcate self-regulation and intellectual curiosity appear to widen the very window through which genetic potential can express itself — a phenomenon increasingly framed as gene-environment correlation. The thirty-million-word gap between affluent and disadvantaged households illustrates how decisively early linguistic input can entrench or erode a child's later prospects.

In my considered view, the dichotomy is itself misleading. Genes may load the proverbial gun, but it is attentive upbringing, contingent upon socio-emotional scaffolding, that pulls the trigger. Particularly during the first five years, when synaptic pruning is most rapid, the rearing environment exerts a disproportionate influence. Policy should accordingly privilege early-years investment over deterministic narratives, recognising that the genome alone scripts no child's biography.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  Band 8 đưa luận điểm interactionist tinh tế ('primary mediator that activates, suppresses or refines') thay vì nghiêng một phía như Band 7, nâng Task Response.

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (cleft 'it is this body of research that', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were genes wholly deterministic', concessive 'Compelling as such data appear') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng vài lần.

•  Band 8 lexis chuyên ngành dày đặc ('hereditarian', 'polygenic scoring', 'synaptic pruning', 'gene-environment correlation', 'inculcate') và cohesion liền mạch ('Notwithstanding', 'by the same token', 'accordingly'), vượt Band 7 ở Lexical Resource lẫn Cohesion.

vocabulary.definition_vi: trụ cột kinh tế của gia đình
vocabulary.example: The father traditionally acted as the breadwinner, while the mother managed the household.
vocabulary.memory_hook: bread (bánh mì, biểu tượng miếng ăn) + winner (người kiếm được) → người kiếm cơm cho cả nhà.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành vi phạm pháp hoặc lệch chuẩn xã hội, đặc biệt ở thanh thiếu niên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The pendulum has swung too far towards permissiveness, which some link to a rise in juvenile **delinquency**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- + linquere (Latin: bỏ mặc) → bỏ mặc bổn phận → hành vi lệch chuẩn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Delinquency' là danh từ trừu tượng (không đếm được); người thực hiện hành vi đó là 'a delinquent'.
vocabulary.definition_en: minor crime or antisocial behaviour, especially committed by young people
vocabulary.definition_vi: hành vi phạm pháp/lệch chuẩn (thường ở thanh thiếu niên)
vocabulary.example: The pendulum has swung too far towards permissiveness, which some link to a rise in juvenile delinquency.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- + linquere (Latin: bỏ mặc) → bỏ mặc bổn phận → hành vi lệch chuẩn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quan hệ huyết thống hoặc mối liên kết bền chặt giống như trong gia đình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Were we to go months without speaking, the **kinship** we share would remain entirely undiminished.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
kin (họ hàng, ruột thịt) + -ship (trạng thái) → mối quan hệ huyết thống.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Kinship' không đếm được; muốn nói về người thân cụ thể thì dùng 'kin' hoặc 'relatives'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being family, or the strong bond that comes from a family-like connection
vocabulary.definition_vi: quan hệ huyết thống, tình thân
vocabulary.example: Were we to go months without speaking, the kinship we share would remain entirely undiminished.
vocabulary.memory_hook: kin (họ hàng, ruột thịt) + -ship (trạng thái) → mối quan hệ huyết thống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ruột thịt, máu mủ — người có quan hệ huyết thống trực tiếp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Even though he chose a different career path, he is still my own **flesh and blood**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
flesh (da thịt) + blood (máu) → những gì cùng chung máu mủ, ruột thịt.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là idiom cố định, không đảo ngược trật tự thành 'blood and flesh'.
vocabulary.definition_en: one's own close relative, connected by direct blood ties
vocabulary.definition_vi: ruột thịt, máu mủ
vocabulary.example: Even though he chose a different career path, he is still my own flesh and blood.
vocabulary.memory_hook: flesh (da thịt) + blood (máu) → những gì cùng chung máu mủ, ruột thịt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Giống nhau một cách rõ rệt, đáng kinh ngạc, đặc biệt về ngoại hình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> So uncanny is the resemblance he **bears** to his late father that strangers occasionally mistake him for him.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
bear (mang) + striking (nổi bật) + resemblance (sự giống nhau) → mang một sự giống nhau nổi bật.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong văn viết học thuật, tránh dùng 'the spitting image of' (khẩu ngữ); nên dùng 'bears a striking resemblance to'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to look very similar to someone, especially a family member
vocabulary.definition_vi: giống nhau một cách rõ rệt/đáng kinh ngạc (về ngoại hình)
vocabulary.example: So uncanny is the resemblance he bears to his late father that strangers occasionally mistake him for him.
vocabulary.memory_hook: bear (mang) + striking (nổi bật) + resemblance (sự giống nhau) → mang một sự giống nhau nổi bật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đồng quan điểm, hợp ý nhau về một vấn đề nào đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Unfortunately, my father and I simply don't **see eye to eye** on politics.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
hai người nhìn thẳng vào mắt nhau (eye to eye) vì cùng chung quan điểm.
collocations: see eye to eye on sth
don't see eye to eye with sb
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng ở thể phủ định 'don't see eye to eye' khi nói về bất đồng; đi với giới từ 'on' + chủ đề.
vocabulary.definition_en: to agree with someone or share the same opinion
vocabulary.definition_vi: đồng quan điểm, hợp ý nhau
vocabulary.example: Unfortunately, my father and I simply don't see eye to eye on politics.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hai người nhìn thẳng vào mắt nhau (eye to eye) vì cùng chung quan điểm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có tính chất di truyền, gia truyền trong dòng họ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Musical talent seems to **run in the family**; everyone plays an instrument.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
một đặc điểm 'chạy' xuyên suốt (run) các thế hệ trong gia đình.
collocations: a trait that runs in the family
vocabulary.common_error: Chủ ngữ phải là đặc điểm/tính trạng (talent, illness), không phải người: 'Musical talent runs in the family', không nói 'He runs in the family'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be a trait or characteristic that many family members share, often passed down through generations
vocabulary.definition_vi: di truyền, có tính chất gia truyền trong dòng họ
vocabulary.example: Musical talent seems to run in the family; everyone plays an instrument.
vocabulary.memory_hook: một đặc điểm 'chạy' xuyên suốt (run) các thế hệ trong gia đình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kẻ lạc loài, thành viên bị coi là hư hỏng hoặc khác biệt so với phần còn lại của gia đình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He was considered the **black sheep** of the family because he dropped out of university.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
một con cừu đen giữa đàn cừu trắng → kẻ khác biệt, bị coi là hư hỏng.
collocations: the black sheep of the family
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn đi kèm 'the' và 'of the family/group'; không dùng số nhiều 'black sheeps' (sheep bất quy tắc).
vocabulary.definition_en: a member of a family or group who is regarded as a disgrace or a failure compared to the others
vocabulary.definition_vi: kẻ lạc loài, thành viên bị coi là hư hỏng/khác biệt trong gia đình
vocabulary.example: He was considered the black sheep of the family because he dropped out of university.
vocabulary.memory_hook: một con cừu đen giữa đàn cừu trắng → kẻ khác biệt, bị coi là hư hỏng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dần trở nên xa cách về mặt tình cảm, thường không có nguyên nhân rõ ràng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After moving to different countries, the siblings began to **drift apart** emotionally.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
drift (trôi dạt) + apart (xa nhau) → từ từ trôi xa nhau như hai con thuyền.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Drift apart' diễn tả quá trình dần dần, khác với 'fall out' (cãi nhau, đoạn tuyệt đột ngột).
vocabulary.definition_en: to gradually become less close to someone emotionally, often without any single dramatic cause
vocabulary.definition_vi: dần trở nên xa cách (về tình cảm)
vocabulary.example: After moving to different countries, the siblings began to drift apart emotionally.
vocabulary.memory_hook: drift (trôi dạt) + apart (xa nhau) → từ từ trôi xa nhau như hai con thuyền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nối gót, tiếp bước theo con đường sự nghiệp hoặc cuộc sống của ai đó, thường là người thân.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She decided to **follow in her mother's footsteps** and become a teacher.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
đặt chân vào đúng dấu chân (footsteps) người đi trước để lại → nối nghiệp.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn cần tính từ sở hữu trước 'footsteps': 'follow in HER mother's footsteps', không bỏ qua.
vocabulary.definition_en: to do the same job or activity as someone else did before, especially a family member
vocabulary.definition_vi: nối gót, tiếp bước theo con đường của ai đó
vocabulary.example: She decided to follow in her mother's footsteps and become a teacher.
vocabulary.memory_hook: đặt chân vào đúng dấu chân (footsteps) người đi trước để lại → nối nghiệp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Gia đình tan vỡ do cha mẹ ly hôn hoặc ly thân, ảnh hưởng đến con cái.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **broken home** can still produce successful children if there is enough support and stability.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
home (mái ấm) bị 'broken' (vỡ) → gia đình tan vỡ do ly hôn/ly thân.
collocations: grow up in a broken home
vocabulary.common_error: Thường đi với động từ 'come from' hoặc 'grow up in', không dùng 'have a broken home'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a family in which the parents are divorced or separated, especially as it affects the children
vocabulary.definition_vi: gia đình tan vỡ, cha mẹ ly hôn/ly thân
vocabulary.example: A broken home can still produce successful children if there is enough support and stability.
vocabulary.memory_hook: home (mái ấm) bị 'broken' (vỡ) → gia đình tan vỡ do ly hôn/ly thân.
